vignette:
Linh's Vigil

Linh Tran was seventy-one when she first came to her therapist's office, though she moved with the careful deliberation of someone much older. She had worked as a financial analyst for thirty-eight years, a career that demanded precision and composure—qualities she had cultivated so thoroughly that colleagues rarely saw the tremor in her hands or understood why she left the office by four o'clock each afternoon without exception. That routine had become non-negotiable in the years since her divorce, a structure that kept her tethered to the parts of her life that still felt manageable.

In 1975, when Linh was twenty-six, the Khmer Rouge had taken her during a forced labor evacuation near Phnom Penh. She had been separated from her family—her husband, her two young daughters—in the chaos of that first night. For eight months, she was held in a labor camp where the line between day and night dissolved into an endless cycle of work, hunger, and the ever-present sound of guards. The worst came near the end of her captivity: a period of three weeks in a makeshift detention cell after she had been accused of hoarding rice. She had been locked in a space so small she could not lie down fully, visited only for interrogation and the distribution of minimal water. When she was finally released back to the work detail, she had been certain she would not survive the next week. By the time the camps were liberated, she had learned a terrible lesson: the institutions and people meant to protect her—the government, the military, the international community she had believed was watching—had abandoned her completely.

She had survived. She had found her way to a refugee camp, eventually to the United States, and eventually to her ex-husband, who had also survived. They had rebuilt a life together, raised their daughters, built careers. But the marriage had fractured under the weight of what neither of them could fully articulate, and they divorced when Linh was sixty-three. Since then, she had lived alone in a small house in a quiet neighborhood, her life organized around work and the careful management of her own mind.

The thought suppression had become automatic by the time she sought help. Whenever an image surfaced—the locked cell, the sound of footsteps approaching, the smell of that place—Linh would immediately redirect her attention. She would pull up spreadsheets on her computer, review financial reports, anything to push the memory back down. But the effort was exhausting, and the memories had begun to seep through in other ways. She found herself lost in counterfactual spirals, especially late at night: if the evacuation had happened an hour later, if she had hidden with the children instead, if the world had intervened sooner. These thoughts would keep her awake until midnight or one in the morning, her mind cycling through variations of a life that never existed, as if she could somehow think her way into a different past.

What frightened her most was the vulnerability of nightfall. During the day, in her office, surrounded by the hum of computers and the presence of other people, she could maintain the illusion of safety. But as darkness came, something shifted in her nervous system. She found it harder to trust that the doors were locked, harder to believe that the world outside her house was not waiting to take her again. She had come to believe that night itself was a threat—that darkness carried the potential for recapture in a way daylight did not. So she stayed up, fighting sleep, keeping watch from her living room window even though she knew intellectually that this made no sense.

The contamination was more recent, and it had begun to interfere with her work. About two years ago, she had started to feel dirty in a way that washing could not address. It was as though the camp itself had left a residue on her skin, something invisible but indelible. She had begun to avoid physical contact—handshakes with colleagues made her skin crawl—and had stopped attending the office holiday parties. More troubling, she had found herself unable to tolerate even minor frustrations. Last month, when a junior analyst had made an error on a report, Linh had felt such a surge of rage and despair that she had excused herself and spent twenty minutes in the bathroom, shaking. She had come to believe that she simply could not manage the ordinary upsets of life, that her capacity to cope had been permanently damaged in that cell.

It was this last incident that had finally brought her in. Her supervisor had gently suggested that she might benefit from talking to someone. Linh had resisted for weeks, but the thought that she might lose her job—the one structure that still held her life together—had frightened her enough to make the appointment.
